IK-789051:L52.text: M. Varadappa Naidu (D) by Lrs. & Anr.

IK-789051:L57.text: R.C. Lahoti, B.N. Srikrishna & G.P. Mathur

IK-789051:L61.text: J U D G M E N T R.C. Lahoti, J.

IK-789051:L62.text: The defendant is in appeal feeling aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, upheld by the High Court, restraining him from interfering with the possession and enjoyment of the suit schedule property by the respondent.

IK-789051:L64.text: The plaintiff and the defendant  both have expired. Their LRs are on record. For the sake of convenience we are making reference to the original parties i.e. the plaintiff and the defendant.

IK-789051:L65.text: The suit property, a piece of land, is situated in Arekempanahally, 36th Division. It appears that the plaintiff and the defendant both claim to be owning two adjoining pieces of land. There is a dispute as to the exact dimensions and shapes (triangular or rectangular) of the pieces of land claimed to be owned and possessed respectively by the two parties. The real dispute, it seems, is about the demarcation of the boundaries of the two pieces of land.

IK-789051:L66.text: However, the fact remains, and that is relevant for our purpose, that the piece of land which forms the subject-matter of the suit is in the possession of the plaintiff-respondent. The plaintiff-respondent was raising construction over the piece of land in his possession, and that was obstructed by the defendant-appellant claiming that the land formed part of his property and was owned by him. The plaintiff filed a suit alleging his title as also his possession over the disputed piece of land.

IK-789051:L67.text: The Trial Court found that although the plaintiff had failed in proving his title, he had succeeded in proving his possession over the suit property which he was entitled to protect unless dispossessed therefrom by due process of law. On this finding the Trial Court issued an injunction restraining the defendant- appellant from interfering with the peaceful possession and enjoyment of the plaintiff-respondent over the suit property.

IK-789051:L68.text: It is contended by the learned counsel for the defendant-appellant that the suit filed by the plaintiff was based on his title. The suit itself was defective inasmuch as declaration of title was not sought for though it was in dispute.

IK-789051:L69.text: Next, it is submitted that if the suit is based on title and if the plaintiff failed in proving his title, the suit ought to have been dismissed without regard to the fact that the plaintiff was in possession and whether the defendant had succeeded in proving his title or not. We find no merit in both these submissions so made and with force.

IK-789051:L70.text: Salmond states in Jurisprudence (Twelfth Edition), "few relationships are as vital to man as that of possession, and we may expect any system of law, however primitive, to provide rules for its protection. . . . . . . Law must provide for the safeguarding of possession. Human nature being what it is, men are tempted to prefer their own selfish and immediate interests to the wide and long-term interests of society in general.

IK-789051:L71.text: But since an attack on a man's possession is an attack on something which may be essential to him, it becomes almost tantamount to an assault on the man himself; and the possessor may well be stirred to defend himself with force. The result is violence, chaos and disorder." (at pp. 265, 266).

IK-789051:L72.text: > "In English Law possession is a good title of right against anyone who cannot show a better. A wrongful possessor has the rights of an owner with respect to all persons except earlier possessors and except the true owner himself. Many other legal systems, however, go much further than this, and treat possession as a provisional or temporary title even against the true owner himself.

IK-789051:L73.text: Even a wrongdoer, who is deprived of his possession, can recover it from any person whatever, simply on the ground of his possession. Even the true owner, who takes his own, may be forced in this way to restore it to the wrongdoer, and will not be permitted to set up his own superior title to it. He must first give up possession, and then proceed in due course of law for the recovery of the thing on the ground of his ownership.

IK-789051:L74.text: The intention of the law is that every possessor shall be entitled to retain and recover his possession, until deprived of it by a judgment according to law." (Salmond, ibid, pp. 294-295) "Legal remedies thus appointed for the protection of possession even against ownership are called possessory, while those available for the protection of ownership itself may be distinguished as proprietary.

IK-789051:L75.text: In the modern and medieval civil law the distinction is expressed by the contrasted terms petitorium (a proprietary suit) and possessorium (a possessory suit)." (Salmond, ibid, p.295) The law in India, as it has developed, accords with the jurisprudential thought as propounded by Salmond. In cite12†Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. Vs.

IK-789051:L76.text: Kumar Naresh Narayan Roy and Ors.  1924 PC 144, Sir John Edge summed up the Indian law by stating that in India persons are not permitted to take forcible possession; they must obtain such possession as they are entitled to through a Court.

IK-789051:L77.text: > The thought has prevailed incessantly, till date, the last and latest one in the chain of decisions being cite13†Ramesh Chand Ardawatiya Vs. Anil Panjwani  (2003) 7 SCC 350. In-between, to quote a few out of severals, in Lallu Yeshwant Singh (dead) by his legal representative Vs. Rao Jagdish Singh and others  (1968) 2 SCR 203, this Court has held that a landlord did commit trespass when he forcibly entered his own land in the possession of a tenant whose tenancy has expired.

IK-789051:L78.text: The Court turned down the submission that under the general law applicable to a lessor and a lessee there was no rule or principle which made it obligatory for the lessor to resort to Court and obtain an order for possession before he could eject the lessee. The court quoted with approval the law as stated by a Full Bench of Allahabad High Court in cite14†Yar Mohammad Vs. Lakshmi Das (AIR 1959 All. 1,4), "Law respects possession even if there is no title to support it.

IK-789051:L79.text: It will not permit any person to take the law in his own hands and to dispossess a person in actual possession without having recourse to a court. No person can be allowed to become a judge in his own cause." In the oft- quoted case of cite15†Nair Service Society Ltd. Vs. K.C.

IK-789051:L80.text: Alexander and Ors.  (1968) 3 SCR 163, this Court held that a person in possession of land in assumed character of owner and exercising peaceably the ordinary rights of ownership has a perfectly good title against all the world but the rightful owner. When the facts disclose no title in either party, possession alone decides.

IK-789051:L81.text: The court quoted Loft's maxim  'Possessio contra omnes valet praeter eur cui ius sit possessionis (He that hath possession hath right against all but him that hath the very right)' and said, "A defendant in such a case must show in himself or his predecessor a valid legal title, or probably a possession prior to the plaintiff's and thus be able to raise a presumption prior in time". In cite16†M.C. Chockalingam and Ors. Vs. V.

IK-789051:L82.text: Manickavasagam and Ors.  (1974) 1 SCC 48, this Court held that the law forbids forcible dispossession, even with the best of title. In Krishna Ram Mahale (dead) by his Lrs. Vs. Mrs. Shobha Venkat Rao  (1989) 4 SCC 131, it was held that where a person is in settled possession of property, even on the assumption that he had no right to remain on the property, he cannot be dispossessed by the owner of the property except by recourse to law. In cite17†Nagar Palika, Jind Vs.

IK-789051:L83.text: Jagat Singh, Advocate  (1995) 3 SCC 426, this Court held that disputed questions of title are to be decided by due process of law, but the peaceful possession is to be protected from the trespasser without regard to the question of the origin of the possession.

IK-789051:L84.text: When the defendant fails in proving his title to the suit land the plaintiff can succeed in securing a decree for possession on the basis of his prior possession against the defendant who has dispossessed him. Such a suit will be founded on the averment of previous possession of the plaintiff and dispossession by the defendant.

IK-789051:L85.text: It is thus clear that so far as the Indian law is concerned the person in peaceful possession is entitled to retain his possession and in order to protect such possession he may even use reasonable force to keep out a trespasser. A rightful owner who has been wrongfully dispossessed of land may retake possession if he can do so peacefully and without the use of unreasonable force.

IK-789051:L86.text: If the trespasser is in settled possession of the property belonging to the rightful owner, the rightful owner shall have to take recourse to law; he cannot take the law in his own hands and evict the trespasser or interfere with his possession.

IK-789051:L87.text: The law will come to the aid of a person in peaceful and settled possession by injuncting even a rightful owner from using force or taking law in his own hands, and also by restoring him in possession even from the rightful owner (of course subject to the law of limitation), if the latter has dispossessed the prior possessor by use of force. In the absence of proof of better title, possession or prior peaceful settled possession is itself evidence of title.

IK-789051:L88.text: Law presumes the possession to go with the title unless rebutted. The owner of any property may prevent even by using reasonable force a trespasser from an attempted trespass, when it is in the process of being committed, or is of a flimsy character, or recurring, intermittent, stray or casual in nature, or has just been committed, while the rightful owner did not have enough time to have recourse to law.

IK-789051:L89.text: In the last of he cases, the possession of the trespasser, just entered into would not be called as one acquiesced to by the true owner.

IK-789051:L90.text: It is the settled possession or effective possession of a person without title which would entitle him to protect his possession even as against the true owner. The concept of settled possession and the right of the possessor to protect his possession against the owner has come to be settled by a catena of decisions. Illustratively, we may refer to cite18†Munshi Ram and Ors. Vs. Delhi Administration  (1968) 2 SCR 455, Puran Singh and Ors. Vs. The State of Punjab  (1975) 4 SCC 518 and Ram Rattan and Ors.

IK-789051:L91.text: Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh  (1977) 1 SCC 188. The authorities need not be multiplied. In cite18†Munshi Ram & Ors. 's case (supra), it was held that no one, including the true owner, has a right to dispossess the trespasser by force if the trespasser is in settled possession of the land and in such a case unless he is evicted in the due course of law, he is entitled to defend his possession even against the rightful owner.

IK-789051:L92.text: But merely stray or even intermittent acts of trespass do not give such a right against the true owner. The possession which a trespasser is entitled to defend against the rightful owner must be settled possession, extending over a sufficiently long period of time and acquiesced to by the true owner. A casual act of possession would not have the effect of interrupting the possession of the rightful owner.

IK-789051:L93.text: The rightful owner may re-enter and re- instate himself provided he does not use more force than is necessary. Such entry will be viewed only as resistance to an intrusion upon his possession which has never been lost. A stray act of trespass, or a possession which has not matured into settled possession, can be obstructed or removed by the true owner even by using necessary force.

IK-789051:L94.text: In Puran Singh and Ors.'s case (supra), the Court clarified that it is difficult to lay down any hard and fast rule as to when the possession of a trespasser can mature into settled possession. The 'settled possession' must be (i) effective, (ii) undisturbed, and (iii) to the knowledge of the owner or without any attempt at concealment by the trespasser. The phrase 'settled possession' does not carry any special charm or magic in it; nor is it a ritualistic formula which can be confined in a strait-jacket.

IK-789051:L95.text: An occupation of the property by a person as an agent or a servant acting at the instance of the owner will not amount to actual physical possession. The court laid down the following tests which may be adopted as a working rule for determining the attributes of 'settled possession' :

IK-789051:L96.text: > i) that the trespasser must be in actual physical possession of the property over a sufficiently long period;

IK-789051:L98.text: > ii) that the possession must be to the knowledge (either express or implied) of the owner or without any attempt at concealment by the trespasser and which contains an element of animus possidendi. The nature of possession of the trespasser would, however, be a matter to be decided on the facts and circumstances of each case;

IK-789051:L99.text: > iii) the process of dispossession of the true owner by the trespasser must be complete and final and must be acquiesced to by the true owner;

IK-789051:L103.text: iv) that one of the usual tests to determine the quality of settled possession, in the case of culturable land, would be whether or not the trespasser, after having taken possession, had grown any crop. If the crop had been grown by the trespasser, then even the true owner has no right to destroy the crop grown by the trespasser and take forcible possession.

IK-789051:L104.text: In the cases of cite18†Munshi Ram and Ors. (supra) and Puran Singh and Ors. (supra), the Court has approved the statement of law made in cite19†Horam Vs.

IK-789051:L105.text: Rex  AIR 1949 Allahabad 564, wherein a distinction was drawn between the trespasser in the process of acquiring possession and the trespasser who had already accomplished or completed his possession wherein the true owner may be treated to have acquiesced in; while the former can be obstructed and turned out by the true owner even by using reasonable force, the latter, may be dispossessed by the true owner only by having recourse to the due process of law for re-acquiring possession over his property.

IK-789051:L106.text: In the present case the Court has found the plaintiff as having failed in proving his title. Nevertheless, he has been found to be in settled possession of the property. Even the defendant failed in proving his title over the disputed land so as to substantiate his entitlement to evict the plaintiff.

IK-789051:L107.text: The Trial Court therefore left the question of title open and proceeded to determine the suit on the basis of possession, protecting the established possession and restraining the attempted interference therewith. The Trial Court and the High Court have rightly decided the suit. It is still open to the defendant-appellant to file a suit based on his title against the plaintiff-respondent and evict the latter on the former establishing his better right to possess the property.

IK-789051:L108.text: The learned counsel for the appellant relied on the Division Bench decision in cite20†Sri Dasnam Naga Sanyasi and Anr. Vs. Allahabad Development Authority, Allahabad and Anr.  AIR 1995 Allahabad 418 and a Single Judge decision in cite21†Kallappa Rama Londa Vs.

IK-789051:L109.text: Shivappa Nagappa Aparaj and Ors.  AIR 1995 Karnataka 238 to submit that in the absence of declaration of title having been sought for, the suit filed by the plaintiff-respondent was not maintainable, and should have been dismissed solely on this ground. We cannot agree.

IK-789051:L110.text: cite20†Sri Dasnam Naga Sanyasi and Anr. 's case relates to the stage of grant of temporary injunction wherein, in the facts and circumstances of that case, the Division Bench of the High Court upheld the decision of the court below declining the discretionary relief of ad-interim injunction to the plaintiff on the ground that failure to claim declaration of title in the facts of that case spoke against the conduct of the plaintiff and was considered to be 'unusual'.

IK-789051:L111.text: In cite21†Kallappa Rama Londa 's case, the learned Single Judge has upheld the maintainability of a suit merely seeking injunction, without declaration of title, and on dealing with several decided cases the learned Judge has agreed with the proposition that where the suit for declaration of title and injunction is filed and the title is not clear, the question of title will have to be kept open without denying the plaintiff's claim for injunction in view of the fact that the plaintiff has been in possession and there is nothing to show that the plaintiff has gained possession by any unfair means just prior to the suit.

IK-789051:L112.text: That is the correct position of law. In cite22†Fakirbhai Bhagwandas and Anr. Vs. Maganlal Haribhai and Anr.  AIR 1951 Bombay 380 a Division Bench spoke through Bhagwati, J. (as his Lordship then was), and held that it is not necessary for the person claiming injunction to prove his title to the suit land. It would suffice if he proves that he was in lawful possession of the same and that his possession was invaded or threatened to be invaded by a person who has no title thereof.

IK-789051:L113.text: We respectfully agree with the view so taken. The High Court has kept the question of title open. Each of the two contending parties would be at liberty to plead all relevant facts directed towards establishing their titles, as respectively claimed, and proving the same in duly constituted legal proceedings. By way of abundant caution, we clarify that the impugned judgment shall not be taken to have decided the question of title to the suit property for or against any of the contending parties.

IK-789051:L114.text: No fault can be found with the judgment and decree appealed against. The appeal is devoid of any merit and is dismissed.

E1.label: M. Varadappa Naidu, original plaintiff-respondent, deceased and represented by legal representatives

E2.label: Rame Gowda, original defendant-appellant, deceased and represented by legal representatives

E3.label: The disputed piece of land constituting the suit schedule property in Arekempanahally, 36th Division; its exact dimensions, shape and relationship to the adjoining claimed properties remain unresolved

E4.label: The plaintiff's attempted construction on the disputed land and the defendant's obstruction of that construction while asserting ownership

F01.text: The Supreme Court described the parties as claiming ownership of adjoining pieces of land and identified uncertainty about their dimensions, shapes and boundary demarcation. This characterizes the dispute without establishing either party's ownership or fixing the disputed boundary.
F01.speaker: Supreme Court of India
F01.quote: The real dispute, it seems, is about the demarcation of the boundaries of the two pieces of land.
limitations: The judgment uses qualified language when describing the apparent underlying boundary dispute.
Neither party's ownership is established by this characterization.
The precise dimensions, shapes and boundaries are not judicially resolved in the supplied reasoning.
The parties' adjoining ownership claims must not be treated as proof of the claimed proprietary boundaries.

F02.text: The plaintiff filed the original suit alleging both title to and possession of the disputed piece of land. TRUE records the making of these allegations, not their substantive truth.
F02.time_scope: Original civil suit; filing date not supplied
F02.speaker: Plaintiff-respondent, as reported by the Supreme Court
F02.quote: The plaintiff filed a suit alleging his title as also his possession over the disputed piece of land.
limitations: The plaintiff's allegation of ownership is not an established proprietary fact.
The allegation of possession is separately evaluated through judicial findings.
The complete original pleadings are not supplied.

F03.text: The Trial Court found that the plaintiff succeeded in proving possession of the identified suit property. The Supreme Court accepted this reported finding as the relevant factual basis for possessory protection.
F03.time_scope: Trial adjudication; exact date not supplied
F03.speaker: Trial Court, as reported and accepted by the Supreme Court
F03.quote: he had succeeded in proving his possession over the suit property
limitations: This establishes an attributed judicial possession finding, not ownership.
The underlying exhibits, testimony and detailed evidentiary assessment are not supplied.
The finding concerns the specific suit property without resolving the larger boundary dispute.
Possession is not independently authenticated outside the judgment.

F04.text: The Trial Court found that the plaintiff failed to prove the title he claimed over the suit property. The Supreme Court expressly acknowledged this finding while preserving the separate possession inquiry.
F04.time_scope: Trial adjudication; exact date not supplied
F04.speaker: Trial Court, as reported and accepted by the Supreme Court
F04.quote: the plaintiff had failed in proving his title
limitations: Failure to prove title is not a finding that the plaintiff's claimed ownership is factually false.
The finding does not establish ownership in the defendant.
The evidence underlying the title determination is not supplied.
The title question was expressly left open.

F05.text: The Supreme Court expressly reported that the plaintiff had been found to be in settled possession of the disputed property notwithstanding his failure to establish title.
F05.time_scope: Possession evaluated in the litigation; precise period not supplied
F05.speaker: Supreme Court of India
F05.quote: Nevertheless, he has been found to be in settled possession of the property.
limitations: The settled-possession classification is expressly reported by the target court.
No case-specific chronology establishing the duration of occupation is supplied.
The judgment does not independently detail every illustrative factor of settled possession.
Owner knowledge, acquiescence, possessory intention and any agricultural activity cannot be independently verified.
Acceptance of the judicial classification is not equivalent to executing the open-text legal test.
The finding does not establish the plaintiff's ownership.

F06.text: The Supreme Court recounted that the defendant obstructed the plaintiff's construction activity on the disputed land while claiming that the land belonged to him. The obstruction and accompanying assertion form one reported episode of interference.
F06.time_scope: During the plaintiff's attempted construction; exact date not supplied
F06.speaker: Supreme Court of India
F06.quote: that was obstructed by the defendant-appellant claiming that the land formed part of his property
limitations: The court reports obstruction of construction as interference with possession.
The defendant's ownership assertion is not proof of his ownership.
The judgment does not independently establish that physical force was actually used.
The exact date, physical method and duration of obstruction are not supplied.
The event must not be multiplied merely because the court separately reports the obstruction and the defendant's accompanying claim.

F07.text: During the reported obstruction, the defendant asserted that the disputed land formed part of his property and belonged to him. TRUE records the existence of that assertion, not the ownership proposition.
F07.time_scope: Same reported construction-obstruction episode as F06
F07.speaker: Defendant-appellant, as reported by the Supreme Court
F07.quote: claiming that the land formed part of his property and was owned by him.
limitations: The claimed ownership is not judicially established.
The claimant's assertion cannot substitute for proof of better title.
This is the ownership assertion accompanying F06, not evidence of a separate transaction.
The statement does not establish the disputed boundary.

F08.text: Counsel for the defendant-appellant argued that the plaintiff's suit was defective because it relied on title while omitting a declaration of title despite the ownership dispute. TRUE records that the procedural and legal objection was advanced.
F08.speaker: Counsel for defendant-appellant
F08.quote: The suit itself was defective inasmuch as declaration of title was not sought for though it was in dispute.
limitations: The defect alleged by counsel is not accepted as a legal conclusion.
The Supreme Court expressly rejected the proposed automatic dismissal.
The complete pleadings have not been independently inspected.
The statement records an argument and does not prove that declaratory relief was legally indispensable.
The objection is evaluated at the merits stage, not automatically under standards governing temporary injunctions.

F09.text: Counsel for the defendant-appellant separately argued that failure to prove the plaintiff's asserted title required dismissal of the suit regardless of the plaintiff's possession or whether the defendant had established his own title.
F09.speaker: Counsel for defendant-appellant
F09.quote: the suit ought to have been dismissed without regard to the fact that the plaintiff was in possession
limitations: TRUE means the argument was made, not that its proposed consequence was correct.
The Supreme Court stated that it found no merit in this submission.
The argument does not negate the judicial possession finding.
The argument is distinct from the defendant's alleged proprietary entitlement.

F10.text: The Supreme Court found that the defendant also failed to prove title over the disputed land sufficient to substantiate his asserted entitlement to evict the plaintiff.
F10.time_scope: Title evaluated in the litigation; exact evidentiary period not supplied
F10.speaker: Supreme Court of India
F10.quote: Even the defendant failed in proving his title over the disputed land so as to substantiate his entitlement to evict the plaintiff.
limitations: The proposition concerns failure of proof, not proof that the defendant lacks all possible ownership rights.
It does not establish proprietary title in the plaintiff.
The defendant's evidence is not independently available for reassessment.
The finding does not predetermine a future properly constituted title action.

F11.text: As recounted by the Supreme Court, the Trial Court deliberately left title unresolved and determined the injunction dispute on the independent basis of established possession.
F11.time_scope: Trial adjudication; exact date not supplied
F11.speaker: Trial Court, as characterized by the Supreme Court
F11.quote: The Trial Court therefore left the question of title open and proceeded to determine the suit on the basis of possession
limitations: The Trial Court's approach is known through the Supreme Court's account.
The original Trial Court judgment is not independently supplied.
A determination based on possession does not resolve ownership.
The lower court's decision to protect possession is not used as independent evidence proving possession.

F12.text: The Supreme Court expressly reported that the High Court had also kept the question of title open.
F12.time_scope: High Court adjudication; exact date not supplied
F12.speaker: High Court, as characterized by the Supreme Court
F12.quote: The High Court has kept the question of title open.
limitations: The proposition is sourced to the Supreme Court's account of the High Court's treatment of title.
The original High Court judgment is not independently supplied.
The reservation cannot be converted into a declaration in favour of either party.

F13.text: The Supreme Court expressly clarified that the impugned judgment did not decide title to the suit property for or against either litigant and that both parties remained free to establish their claimed titles in duly constituted legal proceedings.
F13.speaker: Supreme Court of India
F13.quote: the impugned judgment shall not be taken to have decided the question of title to the suit property for or against any of the contending parties.
limitations: This is an express reservation of title rather than a finding of ownership.
Neither competing proprietary claim is conclusively established or rejected.
Availability of future proceedings does not guarantee admissibility or success in any particular action.
The disputed property and competing rights would require proper identification in future proceedings.

F14.text: The plaintiff's possession was not classified by the target court as merely stray, intermittent or incipient intrusion. This negative classification follows only from the express finding of settled possession and is not independently established by a detailed chronology of occupation.
F14.time_scope: Possession evaluated in the litigation; exact duration unknown
F14.speaker: Supreme Court of India
F14.quote: Nevertheless, he has been found to be in settled possession of the property.
limitations: FALSE is a qualified consequence of the reported judicial settled-possession classification.
The judgment does not provide an independently verifiable chronology excluding every isolated act of trespass.
No particular duration, knowledge, acquiescence or possessory intention is independently proved by this negative classification.
The finding cannot be generalized to other entrants or properties.
The open-text settled-possession test remains a contextual judicial assessment rather than an executable checklist.

L01.text: Applied to the plaintiff and the identified suit property, the judicial finding of possession remains an independent basis for possessory analysis despite the separate finding that the plaintiff failed to prove ownership.
L01.speaker: Supreme Court of India
L01.quote: although the plaintiff had failed in proving his title, he had succeeded in proving his possession over the suit property
limitations: This records the legally relevant distinction supported by F03 and F04.
The proposition does not independently establish the final requirements for an injunction.
The failure of title proof does not determine that the plaintiff is not an owner.
The proposition does not prove the defendant's ownership.
The rule is confined to the same identified suit property.

L02.text: The plaintiff's judicially recognized settled possession supplies a protectable possessory interest against extrajudicial interference. The applicable distinction protects established settled possession even against a person asserting ownership while permitting lawful recovery through appropriate proceedings.
L02.speaker: Supreme Court of India
L02.quote: It is the settled possession or effective possession of a person without title which would entitle him to protect his possession even as against the true owner.
limitations: The case-specific application relies on the target court's settled-possession finding.
Actual ownership by the defendant is not established.
Transient, casual, intermittent or incomplete intrusion is legally distinguished from settled possession.
No rigid temporal threshold or mechanically sufficient combination of illustrative factors is supplied.
The crop-growing illustration for cultivable land is not a universal requirement.
Occupation solely as an owner's agent or servant is distinguished from independent actual possession.
No independent reconstruction of owner knowledge, acquiescence, occupation duration or animus possidendi is possible.
The rule prohibits unauthorized self-help against settled possession but does not prohibit lawful judicial recovery.
The underlying settled-possession classification is open-text and context-sensitive.

L03.text: The plaintiff's legally protectable settled possession, together with the defendant's reported obstruction of construction while asserting ownership, supplies an independent possessory ground for injunctive restraint against interference with that possession. This ground does not require confirmation of the plaintiff's title.
L03.speaker: Supreme Court of India
L03.quote: The law will come to the aid of a person in peaceful and settled possession by injuncting even a rightful owner from using force or taking law in his own hands
limitations: This identifies the possessory ground supporting restraint, not ownership.
It relies on the established possession and obstruction premises, not on the final appellate disposition.
The judgment does not independently prove that physical force was actually used during the obstruction.
The opposing party's assertion of ownership is not proof of actual title.
The rule does not automatically decide every discretionary or procedural requirement governing injunctions.
It does not prevent recovery through due process of law.
The underlying settled-possession classification remains subject to the qualifications represented in L02.

L04.text: The plaintiff's failure to establish title and the defendant's objection concerning the absence of declaratory relief do not automatically defeat an otherwise supportable possessory injunction claim. The Supreme Court rejected the defendant's proposed automatic dismissal while distinguishing the discretionary treatment of temporary injunctions.
L04.speaker: Supreme Court of India
L04.quote: That is the correct position of law.
limitations: The conclusion concerns automatic dismissal based on title non-proof or the alleged omission of declaratory relief.
The independent possessory basis remains necessary.
The Supreme Court's approval of the position discussed in Kallappa Rama Londa does not establish an unconditional rule for all injunction-only suits.
The cited Allahabad decision was distinguished as involving discretionary temporary or ad-interim relief.
The Bombay decision was discussed as authority concerning lawful possession and threatened invasion, not as independent evidence of this case's facts.
The complete pleadings were not supplied for independent verification.
The defendant's rejected arguments remain attributed party claims.
No universal procedural rule governing all disputed-title litigation is reconstructed.
Ownership and precise boundary demarcation remain outside this conclusion.

L05.text: The possessory ground for protecting the plaintiff's settled possession does not itself confirm ownership in the plaintiff or conclusively reject the defendant's possible proprietary claim. The Supreme Court distinguished protection of possession from adjudication of title and expressly preserved that distinction in this case.
L05.speaker: Supreme Court of India

web_review.quote: The Trial Court found that although the plaintiff had failed in proving his title, he had succeeded in proving his possession over the suit property which he was entitled to protect unless dispossessed therefrom by due process of law.
web_review.reason: R1 faithfully represents the distinction between establishing possession and proving proprietary title. The Supreme Court reports that the Trial Court found the plaintiff's possession proved while his title remained unproved, and subsequently endorses deciding the injunction claim on possession without resolving ownership. The ALL connective appropriately combines these two reported findings concerning the same plaintiff and identified suit property. The conclusion is limited to preserving an independent basis for possessory protection; it does not automatically establish entitlement to an injunction or determine ownership. The permitted finding statuses correctly distinguish judicial findings from allegations and independently verified evidence. Failure to prove title is not converted into proof that the plaintiff lacks ownership or that the defendant owns the property. No independent burden allocation or evidentiary standard is introduced. The absence of exception slots is acceptable because this rule preserves a basis for further evaluation rather than granting unconditional protection. Its scope limitations appropriately reserve the disputed boundaries and the additional settled-possession inquiry.

web_review.quote: It is the settled possession or effective possession of a person without title which would entitle him to protect his possession even as against the true owner.
web_review.reason: R2 accurately captures the legal protection of peaceful and settled possession, including possession unsupported by established ownership. The judgment distinguishes effective, settled possession from merely stray, intermittent, casual, or incipient trespass. It recognizes protection against forcible interference by even a rightful owner while permitting legally appropriate resistance to a fresh or incomplete intrusion and preserving judicial recovery. OPEN_TEXT is the correct connective because the judgment expressly resists a rigid formula for classifying settled possession. The reported considerations concerning physical occupation, duration, effectiveness, disturbance, owner knowledge, concealment, possessory intention, completed dispossession, acquiescence, and cultivation are context-sensitive rather than a universally sufficient mechanical conjunction. The transient-trespass exception is material. Its expected FALSE value is defensible only as a consequence of accepting the Supreme Court's reported characterization of the plaintiff's possession as settled; it is not an independently established historical finding about every act of occupation. R2 expressly preserves that distinction and identifies the underlying semantic evaluation as unimplemented. The R1 input narrows the rule to this reconstruction without purporting to define every situation in which settled possession may be protected. The conclusion does not establish the defendant's ownership. The rule correctly avoids inventing a numerical duration, universally mandatory crop requirement, or independent burden standard.

web_review.quote: The law will come to the aid of a person in peaceful and settled possession by injuncting even a rightful owner from using force or taking law in his own hands
web_review.reason: R3 faithfully connects legally protectable settled possession with a possessory basis for injunctive restraint against attempted interference. The Supreme Court recounts that the defendant obstructed the plaintiff's construction while asserting ownership, and endorses protection of the plaintiff's established possession against interference. The ALL connective appropriately requires both a protectable possessory interest and relevant interference with the same property by the identified opponent. The defendant's assertion of ownership remains separate from proof of ownership, and the recorded obstruction does not independently establish that physical force was used. The conclusion is appropriately limited to an independent legal ground for injunction, not automatic satisfaction of every procedural or discretionary requirement. The rule preserves lawful recovery through appropriate proceedings and inherits R2's distinction between settled possession and transient trespass. Its lack of separate exception slots is acceptable within that expressly limited conclusion. web_review.quote: Legal remedies thus appointed for the protection of possession even against ownership are called possessory, while those available for the protection of ownership itself may be distinguished as proprietary.
web_review.reason: R5 faithfully represents the central distinction between possessory and proprietary protection. The Supreme Court invokes the jurisprudential distinction, relates it to Indian law, and expressly clarifies that the impugned judgment does not determine title for or against either litigant. The single-input ALL connective is sufficient for the narrow non-entailment conclusion: an independent possessory basis for injunctive relief does not itself establish ownership. This does not mean possession can never have evidentiary significance for title. The judgment separately recognizes possession or prior peaceful settled possession as evidence of title in the absence of better proof and discusses a rebuttable presumption relating possession to title. R5 properly distinguishes such evidentiary significance from conclusive proprietary adjudication. Its conclusion also does not establish that the opposing party lacks ownership or that independent proprietary adjudication is impossible. The absence of exception slots is appropriate for this limited logical distinction, while the scope limitations preserve the possibility of separate title proceedings. The rule does not invent a conclusive evidentiary presumption, determine the disputed boundary, or introduce an unsupported burden standard.

web_review.quote: It is still open to the defendant-appellant to file a suit based on his title against the plaintiff-respondent and evict the latter on the former establishing his better right to possess the property.

The judgment states that the Trial Court left title open, records that the defendant also failed to establish title sufficient to support his claimed entitlement to evict the plaintiff, and confirms that both parties remain free to establish their respective claimed titles in duly constituted proceedings. The ALL connective combines the distinction established by R5, the express reservation of title, and the defendant's reported non-proof of title. It preserves the express condition that a claimant seeking title-based eviction establish a better right to possess the property. That condition does not establish either party's title now or authorize self-help dispossession. The scope limitations correctly exclude future procedural admissibility, limitation questions, unknown evidence, and unresolved land demarcation.
